entities.name: Temple of Azure Clouds
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Azure Clouds (Biyun Si, 碧云寺) in the Western Hills (Xishan) near Beijing, originally founded during the Yuan Dynasty (circa 1289-1299 CE) and substantially expanded during the Ming Dynasty (particularly during the reign of the Tianqi Emperor, 1620s), is one of the most important Buddhist monasteries in the Beijing region — notable for its dramatic mountain setting in the Fragrant Hills park, its Diamond Throne Pagoda (modeled on the Indian Bodhgaya style), and its historical association with Sun Yat-sen, whose body lay in state here in 1925.

Biyun Si's architectural ensemble develops up a steep hillside on multiple terraces, creating one of the most dramatically situated temple complexes near Beijing. The Diamond Throne Pagoda (1748, built under the Qianlong Emperor) is the artistic highlight — a massive stone platform topped with five pagodas in the Indian mandala style, inspired by the Wutasita (Five-Pagoda Temple) tradition. The Qianlong Emperor expanded the temple extensively as part of his broader pattern of patronizing Buddhist and Tibetan Buddhist establishments.

The temple's modern historical significance comes from Sun Yat-sen's 1925 state lying-in-state here following his death in Beijing. Sun Yat-sen's coffin rested at the temple for four years (1925-1929) while the Nationalist government prepared the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum in Nanjing. The Hall of Five Hundred Arhats, containing 500 individually distinct golden arhat (Buddhist monk) sculptures, is among the most impressive displays of Buddhist devotional art in China.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Azure Clouds — combining Yuan-to-Qing Buddhist history with a dramatic hillside setting, housing Sun Yat-sen's 1925 lying-in-state that connected it to Chinese national history, and featuring a Diamond Throne Pagoda among Beijing's finest Buddhist architecture — is one of Beijing's most historically significant religious sites.
